Friday-Saturday: High pressure briefly amplifies along the WA 
coast today allowing northwest flow to develop over the Inland 
NW. Models are good agreement that Central and Eastern WA will 
be dry with areas of morning fog. A shortwave will drop 
southward along the Continental Divide bringing passing cloud 
cover and light snow showers. Greatest risk will be along the 
Idaho-Montana border as the strongest dynamics remain over 
Western Montana. Snow amounts will vary from a trace to few 
tenths with a 40% chance for an inch over Lookout Pass. 
Motorists traveling over Lookout Pass this afternoon should be 
prepared for variable road conditions with the main band of snow
coming through between 4-8PM. It will be a cold start to the 
day with many areas near or below freezing and only warming into
the upper 30s to low 40s. Benign weather conditions will be in 
place tonight into Saturday afternoon as the ridge slides 
through the region. The pattern is conducive to areas of dense 
fog which is favored across the valleys of NE WA and N ID 
Saturday morning. 

Saturday evening-Sunday night: A shortwave will swing around 
the base of a deep offshore low and eject northeast through the
Inland NW. This will usher a moisture laden cold occluding 
frontal boundary through the inland bringing widespread light 
precipitation with local pockets of moderate intensity. 
Precipitation will spread into Central WA Saturday evening and 
expand east and northeast Saturday night into Sunday morning 
before departing to the north Sunday afternoon-evening. The 
antecedent air mass will be cool such that many areas outside 
the lower Columbia Basin and L-C Valley will experience some 
snow. GFS indicates a broad swath of dendritic omega from -3 to 
-5 along the boundary that leads to moderate confidence for at 
least a 0.01" squeezed out of this boundary region-wide. Areas 
that seem to be in the best location for a tenth or more of 
liquid will be across the upper Columbia Basin close to the Hwy 
2 corridor from the West Plains to the East Slopes northward 
into the Okanogan Highlands and portions of Northeastern WA. 
This area will have added upward motion from divergence aloft 
and potential for a brief convective element if the trailing 
500mb cold pool of -30C can pooch northward into the 
precipitation band steepening lapse rates. Probabilities from 
the East Slopes to Airway Heights for a tenth of QPF varies from
50-80% which loosely equates to similar probabilities for an 
inch or more. Confidence is moderate that this will be a light 
snow event given lack of jet support but wouldn't rule out a few
localized areas receiving 2-3 inches, especially on the higher 
benches around Wauconda Pass, Sherman Pass, Badger Mountain, and
foothills of the East Slopes. The other challenge with this 
event will be temperature profiles at the surface. Mean NBM 
dewpoints for much of the Columbia Basin and into the lower 
elevations around the Palouse and downtown Spokane-Cd'A area are
projected to be around 33F. If this comes to fruition, snow may
struggle to accumulate initially. The overnight timing does add
some confidence for this to be overcome. Overall, the region 
should be prepared for the first winter driving conditions of 
the season if you are traveling Saturday night or Sunday 
morning. Confidence is moderate to high that impacts will be 
minimal by Sunday afternoon.

Monday: Monday is the only day next week with any confidence 
in the forecast with nearly all ensemble models supporting a 
shortwave ridge over the region. This will result in seasonal 
temperatures and areas of low clouds and fog. 


Tuesday-Thursday: There is considerable uncertainty with the forecast 
starting around Tuesday and continuing through the holiday 
week. What we do know, is that the Eastern Pacific will be 
energized with moisture and robust low pressure systems. The 
uncertainty is whether energy from these systems will 
continuously eject inland bringing unsettled weather conditions 
or consolidate and allow a broad downstream ridge develop 
shielding the Inland NW of the active weather pattern. I will 
say that the clusters are leaning toward a middle ground which 
would allow slugs of energy and rich moisture plumes across 
Western WA and toward the Cascades. In these scenarios, we would
have concern for snow over the Cascade passes and portions of 
north-central WA initially but the longer this pattern holds, 
the more likelihood conditions warm and snow, even in the 
mountains changes to rain. If the evolution of this storm track 
wavered just 20-50 miles, it could change the snow levels 
dramatically and Cascade passes could be all snow with each of 
these waves. This would be the least desired for holiday 
travelers and potentially most impactful scenario. The long 
range plumes from the ENS/GEFS for Stevens Pass indicate
